summary.text: 次 is used for “next,” “in sequence,” and “second in rank.” Qin- and Han-period manuscript citations attest ordered and ranked uses. Interpretations of the earliest graph differ.

formation.text: The earliest construction is disputed. One analysis reads an oracle-bone form as a military-station sign, combining an element identified as an early form of 師 with strokes marking an encampment. Other proposals see a person exhaling or a speaking figure with possible saliva marks. Shuowen later analyzes 次 as 欠 plus 二 and assigns 二 a sound role; that account does not resolve the earlier form.

components.text: In Shuowen’s later analysis, 欠 depicts an open-mouthed or exhaling person. Other proposals also describe a breathing or speaking figure, but do not establish 欠 as a component of the earliest graph.
Shuowen assigns 二 a phonetic role in 次. A reported Old Chinese comparison gives similar final sequences, but does not independently establish 二’s identity or role as the sound element.

sound_limitation.text: The reported reconstruction comparison does not independently establish that 二 is the phonetic component in 次.

sound.text: In the Baxter–Sagart Old Chinese system, 二 and 次 have comparable final sequences. This reported comparison is associated with the proposal; it does not establish 二 as 次’s phonetic component.

components.text: In one disputed analysis of an oracle-bone form, this element is identified as an early form of 師 and contributes to a proposed military-station scene. The identification and scene are interpretations, not settled readings of the graph.

In the same disputed oracle-bone analysis, two strokes mark an encampment or station. This proposed indicator belongs to that historical interpretation, not to the established modern component analysis.

history.text: Oracle-bone and bronze examples are recorded, followed by Qin-slip, seal, clerical, and regular-script forms. One analysis interprets an oracle-bone graph as an early form of 師 combined with strokes marking an encampment, hence a military-station sign. Other interpretations differ, so the proposed scene remains uncertain.

Some bronze forms are described as having marks below 欠 or short strokes. It is unclear whether this reflects regularization, corruption, or a meaningful graphic change. Shuowen later analyzes 次 as 欠 plus 二 and assigns 二 a sound role, an account that remains disputed.

uncertainties.text: Interpretations of the earliest graph differ: proposals include a military-station sign, a person exhaling, and a speaking figure with possible saliva marks. These alternatives remain unresolved.
Shuowen’s analysis of 二 as a sound element is historically important, but the reported reconstruction comparison does not independently confirm that role.

No securely dated semantic path connects a proposed early meaning to “next” or “in sequence.” The lodging and tent examples come from transmitted texts whose witnesses are not dated in the cited accounts.

senses.gloss: in sequence; next or second in rank
senses.text: Qin- and Han-period manuscript citations attest 次 for ordered transmission and successive rank. These uses are established by that period, but do not show that they were the graph’s original meaning.
Transmitted texts use 次 for lodging or tents. How these uses relate to ranked and ordered meanings is unresolved.

A Han silk manuscript is reported to use 次 to write 恣. This is a proposed sound-based reuse of the graph for a different word, not a change in 次’s meaning; the cited account gives no pronunciations to demonstrate the resemblance.

A Mawangdui manuscript is reported to use 次 where the transmitted Zhouyi has 濟. This is a proposed sound-based reuse of the graph for a different word, not a change in 次’s meaning; the cited account gives no pronunciations to demonstrate the resemblance.

limitations.text: The Qin- and Han-period attestations do not establish the first occurrence of ordered or ranked uses, or their derivation from any proposed original sense. No semantic link is asserted where the evidence does not demonstrate one.
次 is reported in place of 恣 and 濟 in separate manuscripts, but the cited material gives no pronunciations to demonstrate or independently assess the proposed sound-based borrowings.

overview.text: 次 means “next,” “in order,” or “second in rank.” Qin- and Han-period manuscripts attest ordered and ranked uses; interpretations of the earliest graph differ.

components.text: In Shuowen’s analysis, 欠 pictures an open-mouthed or exhaling person; this does not settle the earliest graph’s form.
Shuowen treats 二 as a sound element. A reported comparison motivates that proposal, but does not prove 二 supplied 次’s sound.
One disputed oracle-bone reading identifies this element as an early form of 師, part of a proposed military-station scene.
In that reading, two strokes mark an encampment or station; this interpretation of the old graph remains disputed.

relationships.text: In Shuowen’s analysis, 欠 pictorially represents an open-mouthed or exhaling person within 次.
Shuowen analyzes 二 as the phonetic element in 次; this role remains disputed.
One analysis of an oracle-bone form identifies an element as an early form of 師 and interprets it as part of a military-station scene.
One analysis of an oracle-bone form interprets two strokes as an indicator of an encampment or station.
